title.en: Unit 2 · Collecting Data, Sampling & Experimental Design

body.en: Sound statistical conclusions require well-designed data collection. Observational studies identify associations; randomized experiments can establish cause-and-effect relationships. Randomization is the essential tool for eliminating selection bias and balancing confounding variables.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Sampling Strategies & The Role of Randomness

body.en: Identify and contrast common sampling designs: Simple Random Sampling (SRS), stratified sampling, cluster sampling, and systematic sampling.

MethodProcedureKey Advantage
Simple Random (SRS)Every group of size \(n\) has equal probability of selectionCompletely unbiased, gold standard
Stratified RandomDivide population into homogeneous groups (strata); take SRS within each stratumReduces sampling variability between strata; guarantees representation
Cluster SamplingDivide into heterogeneous clusters (mini-populations); randomly select whole clustersCost-effective and practical for geographically dispersed units
Systematic SamplingSelect every \(k\)-th individual after a random starting pointSimple to implement; avoids clustering
Convenience / VoluntarySelect whoever is easily available or self-selectedExtremely biased — invalid for inference

A high school has 400 freshmen, 350 sophomores, 320 juniors, and 300 seniors. An administrator randomly selects 25 students from each grade level to survey opinion on a school schedule change. Identify the sampling design and explain why it is advantageous.

This is a stratified random sample. The grades represent homogeneous strata with respect to high school experience. Stratifying guarantees equal representation from each grade level and reduces sampling variability compared to a simple random sample.

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

An airline wants to inspect passenger satisfaction. It randomly selects 10 flights departing from a major hub on a given day and surveys every passenger on those 10 flights. Identify this sampling method and distinguish it from stratified sampling.

solution.en:
This is a cluster sample.

In cluster sampling, the population is divided into clusters (individual flights), a random sample of whole clusters is selected, and all individuals within those clusters are surveyed. In stratified sampling, individuals from every group would be sampled, whereas here, entire flights are either completely included or completely excluded.

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Principles of Experimental Design & Matched Pairs

body.en: Apply the four pillars of experimental design (comparison, random assignment, control, replication) and design randomized block and matched-pairs experiments.

label.en: ● The Four Core Principles of Experimental Design

body.en:
• 1. Comparison: Use two or more treatment groups (or a treatment and a control/placebo) to ensure differences are due to the treatments rather than external time trends.
  • 2. Random Assignment: Use chance methods to assign subjects to treatment groups. This creates roughly equivalent groups by balancing lurking/confounding variables.
  • 3. Control: Keep other variables identical across all groups to prevent them from confounding the results.
  • 4. Replication: Apply treatments to enough experimental units so that genuine differences between treatment effects can be distinguished from chance variation.

A researcher wants to evaluate a new memory supplement. 60 volunteers are paired based on baseline memory test scores (the two highest scores paired, the next two highest paired, etc.). Within each pair, a coin flip assigns one subject to the supplement and the other to an identical placebo. What is this experimental design called, and what is its primary benefit?

This is a matched-pairs design (a specialized form of randomized block design). Its primary benefit is that it controls for baseline memory differences among participants, drastically reducing experimental variability and increasing the power to detect any true effect of the supplement.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Explain why random assignment of treatments is required to establish cause-and-effect, while random selection of subjects is required to generalize results to a larger population.

solution.en:
Random Assignment: Balances out confounding variables across treatment groups so that any observed difference in the response variable can be attributed solely to the treatments, thereby establishing cause-and-effect.

Random Selection: Ensures that the sample is representative of the broader population without systematic selection bias, allowing conclusions to be generalized to the population.

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Sources of Bias, Confounding & Scope of Inference

body.en: Diagnose subtle forms of bias (undercoverage, nonresponse, response bias), distinguish confounding from common response, and correctly delineate the scope of statistical inference.

label.en: ▲ AP Exam Traps & Pitfalls — Sampling & Experimentation

body.en:
• Nonresponse vs. Voluntary Response: Nonresponse occurs when selected individuals in a scientific sample fail to participate. Voluntary response occurs when the sample consists entirely of self-selected volunteers who chose to respond (e.g. online polls).
  • Confounding Variable Definition: A confounding variable is associated with the explanatory variable AND affects the response variable, making it impossible to separate its effect from the treatment effect. Always name both associations when asked to identify confounding on the AP exam!
  • Scope of Inference Matrix:
    Random Selection?Random Assignment?Valid Inferences
    YesYesInference about population AND cause-and-effect
    NoYesCause-and-effect ONLY (for participants only)
    YesNoInference about population ONLY (association only)
    NoNoNo generalization and no causal inference

An observational study finds that people who drink green tea regularly have a lower incidence of cardiovascular disease than non-tea drinkers. Can the researchers conclude that green tea consumption causes a reduction in heart disease risk? Identify a possible confounding variable.

No, causal conclusions cannot be established from an observational study because treatments were not randomly assigned. A plausible confounding variable is overall lifestyle / diet: regular green tea drinkers may exercise more frequently and eat healthier diets than non-tea drinkers, which independently lowers cardiovascular disease risk.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

A university randomly selects 500 alumni from its registry and mails them a questionnaire asking about their starting salary. Only 95 alumni return the completed questionnaire. (a) What specific type of bias is present? (b) In what direction is the estimated mean starting salary likely to be biased, and why?

solution.en:
(a) Nonresponse Bias: A scientifically selected sample was contacted, but a large majority (405 out of 500, or 81%) failed to respond.

(b) Upward (overestimate) Bias: Alumni with high-paying prestigious jobs are generally much more willing and proud to report their earnings, while alumni who are unemployed or earn modest salaries are less likely to respond. Therefore, the sample mean salary is likely to be an overestimate of the true population mean salary.
